title: Depression's Physical Signature
hook: Low mood is not only a feeling; it can slow the walk, stoop the spine and quiet the voice, and others often see it before the person names it.
why:
The World Health Organization estimated that around 280 million people were living with depression in 2019, about one adult in twenty. Most of them were not in a doctor's office. They were at work, at the school gate, at the dinner table, and the people around them saw something before anyone used a word for it: a slower walk, a quieter voice, a man who had stopped shaving or stopped coming to the pub.

This chapter teaches what low mood can do to the body, so that you can notice it in the people you care about, and in yourself. It draws on research into how depression changes walking, speech, the face and daily habits. It is also, more than any chapter so far, a chapter about limits. Every sign described here has many other causes, and none of them, alone or together, is a diagnosis. Your job is not to decide what is wrong. It is to notice that something has changed, to ask, to stay, and to help the person reach someone who can find out.

teach.h: Low mood lives in the body too.
teach.p:
Depression is often described as a disorder of mood, but the standard clinical descriptions include much more than sadness. They include changes in sleep, in appetite and weight, in energy, in concentration, and in movement: a slowing down, or sometimes a restless agitation. A person can feel little sadness at all and still be depressed, describing instead a flatness, a heaviness, a loss of interest in things that used to matter.

That is why the body is often where depression first becomes visible to others. The person may not recognise their own low mood, especially if it has come on slowly, and many men in particular describe it in physical terms first: tiredness, aches, poor sleep, feeling run down. The chapter on the I'm Fine mask described how distress in men can also show as irritability, drinking or withdrawal.

For a reader, this means looking at the whole person over time: not one bad day, but a pattern lasting weeks. Doctors who assess depression typically look for changes that have lasted at least a couple of weeks, and that represent a real change from how the person used to be.

It also means holding every observation loosely. Tiredness, slowness and poor sleep come with many physical illnesses, with grief, with overwork, with new babies and with ageing. What you are looking for is not a sign but a change, sustained, across several areas of life, in someone whose baseline you know.

The body often speaks first. Your job is to hear it as a question, not an answer.
teach.disconfirm: If depression showed itself only in what people said about their mood, with no reliable changes in sleep, energy or movement, the body would be no guide at all. The clinical descriptions and the research below both suggest that bodily changes are common.

teach.h: The walk slows and the body bends.
teach.p:
In 2009 Johannes Michalak and colleagues used motion-capture equipment to record how people walked. Compared with people who had never been depressed, patients with depression walked more slowly, swung their arms less, and moved their heads and upper bodies up and down less with each step. They also tended to walk with a more slumped, forward-leaning posture. People induced into a sad mood in the laboratory showed a milder version of the same pattern.

In 2021 the same research group took the question out of the laboratory, fitting patients with sensors during ordinary daily life. Patients again walked more slowly, with less up-and-down movement and a more slumped posture. Interestingly, moments of faster, bouncier walking tended to be followed by slightly better mood, which raises the possibility that the link runs in both directions, though this is far from a treatment.

You can see these changes without any equipment. A friend who used to stride now shuffles. A father who used to walk ahead of the family now lags behind. A colleague's step on the stairs sounds heavier. The chapter on the spine as status described how posture tracks recent success and failure; this is a slower, longer version of the same slump.

As always, compare with the person's own baseline and consider other causes. Injury, arthritis, illness, medication, fatigue and simply getting older all slow the walk. A gait that has changed over weeks, without an obvious physical reason, alongside changes elsewhere, is worth noticing.
teach.disconfirm: If people with depression walked just as quickly and upright as others, in the laboratory and in daily life, gait would tell you nothing. Both studies found differences, though they were averages across groups, not a test that works on any one person.

teach.h: The voice slows and the pauses lengthen.
teach.p:
The chapter on voice described how voices carry the body's state. Depression has its own vocal pattern. In 2012 James Mundt and colleagues recorded the speech of over a hundred adults with depression during a treatment study. People with more severe depression tended to speak more slowly and to pause for longer. Those who responded to treatment began to speak faster, with shorter pauses, as they improved.

Other research has described a flatter voice, with less rise and fall in pitch, lower volume, and less energy, the kind of voice people describe as monotonous or tired. Conversations with someone in a low period often feel effortful: answers come late, are short, and trail off. Laughter becomes rare.

These changes are especially visible on the phone, where the voice is all you have. The chapter on voice described a father who noticed his son's voice had gone slow and flat on their weekly call; that kind of change, against a well-known baseline, is often the first sign anyone notices.

The usual cautions apply with force. Some people always speak slowly. Tiredness, illness, medication, a language that is not the speaker's first and simple shyness all slow and flatten speech. And the research findings are averages across groups; the links between any single voice feature and depression severity are modest. A slow voice is not a symptom. A voice that has slowed, against its own baseline, alongside other changes, is a reason to ask.

Listen for the slowing more than for the slowness.
teach.disconfirm: If people's speech did not change as their low mood deepened or lifted, voice would be no guide. The treatment study found it did, on average, though the associations were modest and cannot be applied to a single person as a test.
teach.pullQuote: Listen for the slowing more than for the slowness.

teach.h: The face quiets and the gaze drops.
teach.p:
Studies that code facial movement during conversations with people who are depressed tend to find less movement overall: fewer smiles, and briefer ones; less animation; more time with the face at rest. When smiles do appear, they are more often polite smiles with the mouth alone, the kind the chapter on the face described. The gaze tends to drop, and eye contact becomes shorter and rarer.

The face plate in this block shows mouth movements that sometimes appear in low mood: the lips pressed, the corners drawn down, the chin pushed up. They are shown as movements, not as signs of depression, because each of them appears in many other states too: concentration, doubt, disapproval, effort.

The quieting of the face is easy to misread. People may take it as coldness, boredom or disapproval, and respond by withdrawing themselves, which deepens the isolation that low mood already brings. A man who seems uninterested in his friends may be finding it hard to feel interest in anything.

Faces also differ in their resting state for reasons that have nothing to do with mood. Some people have naturally still faces. Conditions such as Parkinson's disease reduce facial movement, as the chapter on the face noted. Autistic people may move their faces differently. A still face is not a sad face. A face that has gone still, compared with how it used to be, is a change.

If someone's face has stopped lighting up, do not take it personally. Wonder what has dimmed it.
teach.disconfirm: If people in low periods showed just as much facial movement and eye contact as others, the face would not help. Research coding facial movement has found reductions on average, though faces vary so much at rest that only a change from baseline means anything.

teach.p:
Not everyone slows down. Some people with low mood become restless and agitated: pacing, wringing their hands, unable to sit still, picking at their skin or nails. This is sometimes called psychomotor agitation, and it can look like anxiety or anger more than sadness.

Other changes show in daily life rather than in movement. Self-care slips: shaving, washing, laundry, the state of the house or the car. Clothes stay the same for days. Meals are skipped, or replaced by snacks and drink, and weight changes in either direction. Sleep changes too: some people wake very early and cannot get back to sleep, others sleep far longer than usual and still wake exhausted. Energy drains, so that small tasks feel enormous.

People who live or work alongside someone often see these changes before anyone else: the post left unopened, the lunch not eaten, the man who has stopped going to the gym, the friend who cancels more often than he comes.

Each of these, again, has many ordinary causes. Unopened post can mean a busy month. Early waking can come with stress, ageing or a new baby. Weight loss can mean a physical illness that needs a doctor quickly. That is part of why the right response to these signs is never your own conclusion but a suggestion that the person sees a doctor, who can look for physical causes as well as low mood.

The small things that slip are often the first things anyone can see.
teach.disconfirm: If changes in self-care, sleep and appetite were no more common in people with low mood than in anyone else, they would carry no information. The clinical descriptions include them precisely because they are common, but each also has many physical causes.

teach.h: None of this is a diagnosis.
teach.p:
This block is short because it needs to be unmistakable. Nothing in this chapter can tell you that someone is depressed. Not the walk, not the voice, not the face, not the sleep, and not all of them together.

Many conditions produce the same picture. Grief, described later in this part, slows the body and quiets the face. Physical illnesses, including thyroid problems, anaemia, diabetes, infections, heart conditions and some cancers, cause fatigue, slowness and weight change. Many medications have similar effects. Overwork and lack of sleep can produce almost every sign described here. Some people are simply quieter, slower and more inward than others, and always have been.

Labelling someone as depressed, to their face or to others, can do real harm. It can feel like an accusation. It can spread through a workplace and follow the person for years. It can be wrong. And it takes from the person the chance to describe their own experience in their own words.

What you can say, honestly, is what you have noticed: *You've seemed slowed down lately, and you've not been coming out.* What you can do is ask how they are, stay with the answer, and encourage them to see a doctor, who is trained to tell these things apart. That is not a lesser role than diagnosis. It is the role most likely to help.

Notice, ask, stay, refer. Leave the naming to the person and their doctor.
teach.disconfirm: If people trained in nothing but observation could reliably tell depression apart from grief, illness, medication and fatigue by watching someone, this block would be too cautious. Even clinicians rely on conversation, history and sometimes tests, not on appearance alone.

teach.h: Ask, stay, and help them reach a doctor.
teach.p:
When you have noticed changes in someone close to you, the chapter on the I'm Fine mask described how to ask: privately, side by side, specifically about what you have seen, with an exit, and twice if needed. With low mood, a few more things help.

Be patient with the pace. People in low periods often answer slowly, and may struggle to explain what is wrong. Long pauses are not refusals. Do not fill them, and do not hurry the person towards a conclusion.

Avoid the phrases that make it worse: *cheer up*, *look on the bright side*, *other people have it worse*, *you just need to get out more*. Each tells the person that their state is a choice they are failing to make. Offer company instead, and small practical help: a walk, a meal, a lift, a task taken off their list. Low mood shrinks the world; small invitations widen it a little.

Encourage a doctor, and make it practical: offer to help find the number, to book the appointment, to go along. Say plainly that low mood is common and that treatments, including talking therapies, medication, and support with exercise and sleep, help many people.

If the person talks about hopelessness, about being a burden, about not wanting to be here, or if you are worried for their safety, ask them directly whether they are thinking about suicide. The chapter on suicidal ideation explains how, and the crisis resources are one tap away. Asking will not put the idea in their head. It may be the thing that lets them say it.
teach.disconfirm: If people in low periods recovered just as well when those around them said *cheer up* as when they offered company, patience and practical help towards a doctor, the advice in this block would not matter. The experience of most people who have been through depression suggests that it does.

poseGallery.doCaption: Sitting with him, and asking how long it has felt like this.
poseGallery.annotation: Telling someone to cheer up suggests their mood is a choice they are failing to make. Company and patience help more.

poseGallery.doCaption: Seeing a slowed walk and voice as a change from who he was.
poseGallery.annotation: Depression often slows movement and speech. Measured against the person's own baseline, slowness is a reason to ask, not to judge.

poseGallery.doCaption: Waiting through them, without filling the silence.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Hurrying him through the long pauses.
poseGallery.annotation: People in low periods often answer slowly. A long pause is not a refusal, and hurrying it closes the door.

poseGallery.doCaption: Telling him, privately, what you have noticed.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Telling the team he is depressed.
poseGallery.annotation: Labels can harm, spread and be wrong. Describe what you have seen to the person himself, and leave the naming to him and his doctor.

caseStudy:
Kevin, forty-one, notices it first on the phone. His older brother Neil, fifty-six, was made redundant in the spring after thirty years at the same firm. Neil used to ring on Sundays and talk for an hour. Now Kevin rings him, and the calls are short. Neil's voice is slow and flat, his answers come after long pauses, and he never laughs.

When Kevin visits in June, he sees more. Neil walks to the shop with him slowly, slightly stooped, letting Kevin get ahead. He has not shaved for days. There is unopened post on the hall table. He says he is just tired, sleeping badly, waking at four every morning. Their mother tells Kevin that Neil has let himself go and needs to pull himself together.

Kevin suggests a walk along the river they used to fish as boys. Side by side, after a while, he says that Neil has seemed slowed down since the job went, and asks how he really is. A long silence. Then Neil says that nothing seems to matter, that he does not enjoy anything, and that he feels like a waste of space. Kevin asks him, plainly, whether he has had thoughts of not wanting to be here, or of ending his life. Neil looks at him, surprised, and says no, not that, but he has felt flat like this for months.

Kevin tells him that it sounds like more than tiredness, that it is common after a big loss like a job, and that he thinks Neil should see his doctor. He offers to sit with him while he rings. Neil agrees, and the doctor sees him that week, runs some blood tests to rule out physical causes, and refers him for talking therapy.

Kevin starts driving over on Saturday mornings for a walk. In August, on the phone, Neil laughs at something. Kevin writes it down.
observe: Think of three people you see or speak to regularly and notice whether anyone's walk, voice or habits have slowed over the past few months.
On your next phone call with someone you know well, notice their pace of speech and the length of their pauses compared with usual.
Notice the phrases you tend to reach for when someone seems low, and whether any of them suggest the mood is a choice.

drills.name: Baseline Memory
steps: Choose two people close to you and write down how they usually walk, talk, laugh and look after themselves.
Write down anything that has changed over the past few months.
For each change, list at least three possible causes, including physical ones.
Mark any person with several changes lasting more than a couple of weeks.
Write one behaviour-first question you could ask that person.

drills.name: Phone Voice
steps: On your next few calls with people you know well, listen to the pace of their speech and the length of their pauses.
Notice their laughter, and how much their pitch rises and falls.
Compare each with how they usually sound.
Write down any change you notice.
If a voice has changed and other things have too, plan a time to see the person in person.

drills.name: Phrases Audit
steps: Write down everything you have ever said, or heard said, to someone who was low, such as cheer up or you'll feel better soon.
Mark each phrase that suggests the mood is a choice or a failure.
For each marked phrase, write a replacement that offers company, patience or practical help.
Say the replacements aloud.
Keep the list somewhere you will see it.

drills.name: The Practical Path
steps: Find out exactly how to book a doctor's appointment where you live, including any online system.
Find out whether talking therapies can be accessed directly where you live, and note how.
Find the crisis resources in this app for your region.
Write three practical offers you could make to someone who needs a doctor.
Rehearse saying one of them aloud.

drills.name: Your Own Signature
steps: Think back to a period when your own mood was low.
Write down what changed in your body and habits: sleep, appetite, walk, voice, self-care, drinking.
Write down who noticed, if anyone, and what they did.
Write the first change that appeared, before you knew anything was wrong.
Note one person you would want to tell if that change appeared again.

quiz.q: Your father has been walking more slowly and talking less for several weeks. What can you reasonably conclude?
options: That he is depressed, and needs to be started on medication soon
That he is simply getting older, and nothing more needs to be done
That something has changed; it has many causes, so ask and suggest a doctor
That he is angry with the family about something and is withdrawing
quiz.explain: Slowing has many causes, including physical illness, grief, medication and low mood. A sustained change is a reason to ask how he is and to suggest a doctor, who can look for physical causes too. It is never a diagnosis.

quiz.q: What did Michalak and colleagues find when they recorded how people with depression walked?
options: Slower walking, less arm swing and less up-and-down movement
Faster walking, as if they were trying to escape from something
No difference at all from people who had never been depressed
A stiff, upright posture with the head held unusually high
quiz.explain: Patients walked more slowly, swung their arms less, bounced less and leaned forward more, and a later study found the same in daily life. These are group averages, not a test for any one person.

quiz.q: What did Mundt and colleagues find about speech in people being treated for depression?
options: Speech was unaffected by depression at any level of severity
Depressed people spoke faster and with fewer pauses than others
Only the pitch of the voice changed, never the pace of speaking
Severe depression went with slower speech and longer pauses
quiz.explain: More severe depression went with slower speech and longer pauses, and people who improved began speaking faster. The associations were modest, so the change from a person's own baseline matters more than any single feature.

quiz.q: A friend who has seemed low for about a month says he sometimes wonders what the point of anything is. What fits this chapter?
options: Tell him everyone feels like that sometimes, and change the subject
Ask him directly whether he has had thoughts of suicide, and stay
Tell him he should cheer up, since he has a lot to live for
Wait to see whether he mentions it again before doing anything
quiz.explain: Talk of pointlessness after weeks of low mood is a reason to ask directly about suicide. Asking does not plant the idea, and it may let him say what he has been carrying. Then stay with him, and help him reach a doctor or crisis line.

quiz.q: Why can none of the signs in this chapter be used to diagnose depression?
options: Because depression has no physical signs at all, only feelings
Because only very severe depression ever shows in the body
Because each sign has many other causes, such as illness or grief
Because people with depression always hide the signs from others
quiz.explain: Physical illness, grief, medication, overwork and temperament can all produce slowing, quietness, sleep change and self-neglect. Telling them apart takes a doctor, conversation and sometimes tests.

quiz.q: A colleague has become slow, quiet and unkempt over several weeks. A manager wants to tell the team he is depressed so they will make allowances. What fits?
options: Talk to him privately about what you have noticed; his health is his to share
Support the manager, since the team will be kinder if they understand
Ask the team whether anyone else has noticed he seems depressed lately
Say nothing to anyone, since it is not your place to notice such things
quiz.explain: Labels can harm, spread and be wrong, and his health is his to share. Raising what you have noticed with him privately, and encouraging him towards a doctor, respects him and helps far more.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific person you know, or yourself, who went through a low period. Describe what changed in the body and daily life, as behaviour: walk, voice, face, sleep, appetite, self-care. Who noticed first, and what did they do? Looking back with this chapter in mind, what would you have wanted someone to say, and when? Then write the words you would use, privately and side by side, to someone showing similar changes now.
reflection.guidance: Many men find their example in their own history, and that is valuable: it tells you what your own early signs are. Describe changes as behaviour, and resist naming a diagnosis. The words you write at the end should describe what you noticed, ask how the person is, and leave room for them to answer slowly.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to read low mood as a character flaw: laziness, coldness, ingratitude, a man who has let himself go. The second is the opposite: deciding that someone is depressed from what you have seen and saying so, to them or to others, when grief, illness, medication or temperament could explain it all. The third is to say the phrases that make it worse, *cheer up*, *look on the bright side*, which imply the mood is a choice. The fourth is to notice and do nothing, waiting for the person to raise it, when low mood makes raising things hardest. And the most serious is to hear talk of hopelessness or being a burden and move on. Notice, ask, stay, help them reach a doctor, and if you are worried, ask directly about suicide.
